records.name: Vanuatu
records.summary:
Vanuatu demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) with no legal gender recognition; there is a small VPride community in Port Vila, and kastom and church conservatism — but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

Direct risk signals for visitors: in November 2024 the government moved to develop a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion, framed as contrary to constitutional and Christian values, and the Marriage Act was amended to define marriage as the union of a male and a female, so same-sex marriages cannot be registered — a partner-travel consideration.

sources.summary: Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

RNZ (18 Nov 2024): Parliament amended the Marriage Act to define marriage as the union of a male and a female; Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed same-sex marriages cannot be registered, and pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law.

RNZ (5 Nov 2024): Ministry of Justice and Community Services to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion; National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, framing V-Pride as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values — direct risk signal for visibly LGBT/trans visitors.

records.name: Nauru
records.summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.summary: US Mission Geneva (Mar 2011): publishes the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation & gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries — Nauru is among the signatories (with Fiji, Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others). For this record: dated evidence of Nauru's diplomatic position supporting SOGI rights.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours. For this record: a comparative-index placement for Nauru.

The Guardian (29 May 2016), headline-level (article body did not survive retrieval — nav shell only): 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide' — the 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions repealed, replacing them including attempted-suicide provisions. For this record: the dated decriminalisation event.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information. For this record: the current legal-status snapshot for trans/intersex people specifically.
